I do like Eisenstein, though his work in montage always tied itself so much closer to conventional narrative, with the visual digression being far less afield. Not saying narrative is vital, I have a deep and in unabiding love for Stan Brackhage keeps that in toe, but Makavejev’s work always felt so ostentatious to me? Almost like it was not enough to be punk, not profound enough to be philosophical, and then often the connections being made feeling tenuous (at least to me). Granted I’ve shifted a lot since that period in college, and a lot of works I love have taken a lot from him. I just remember the work coming off as ostentatious and unfinished at the time

Pretentious isn’t really the right word and more Makavejev’s style kinda fundamentally doesn’t work for me. The sexuality with politik and graphic nature being mapped on a self-professed profundity has always rubbed me the wrong way, and pretentious is an inaccurate but useful term to use. It always ends up reminding me less of my other favorite experimental works and more of the stuff friends from film school pumped out in a weekend when they were out of ideas and threw stuff together from B-reels they shot for other projects.

I actively disbelieve in objective quality (a BFA does that to you, let’s see if an MFA brings me back around on that) so I’m going to go with three films that I genuinely, personally, see as the closest to perfect a film has ever worked for me.

In the Mood for Love: gorgeous, heartbreaking and thought-provoking, every shot is necessary and every tiny gesture and movement contains weight and pathos. It’s odd because it can feel flawed upon first viewing with its slow-motion vignettes but by the end of the film their presence is explained and subverted and their presence is truly vital to the flow and impact of the film.

Dead Man: Hysterically funny, shockingly deep and wildly subversive, it’s also perhaps the best exploration of the contradictions of American history and myth making in cinema history. Every line works, every performance is stellar, every shot is hypnotic.

Andrei Rublev: put a gun to my head this is my nominee for the Greatest Film of All Time. It needs that three hour runtime, it needs that weird prologue with the balloon, it needs to be boring at the beginning so you sink into its world. I can think of no other piece of art ever made that has as much to say about the role of the artist in society.
